data.title: Choose the correct answer for each question.
data.description: Practise the Zero Conditional for general truths and the First Conditional for real future possibilities.
learningPoints: Use the Zero Conditional for facts, rules and things that are generally true.
Use Present Simple in both clauses of the Zero Conditional.
Use the First Conditional for a real future possibility.
Use Present Simple after if and will + base verb in the result clause.
Do not normally use will directly after if in a First Conditional.
Choose the conditional form that matches fact versus future possibility.

sections.summary: Using the Zero Conditional for a general truth.
sections.explain: Use IF + Present Simple, Present Simple for facts and general truths.

words.word: If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.
If you will heat water to 100°C, it boils.
If you heat water to 100°C, it will always boiled.

sections.summary: Using the Zero Conditional for a routine result.
sections.explain: The Zero Conditional describes a result that regularly follows a condition.

words.word: If I drink coffee at night, I don't sleep well.
If I will drink coffee at night, I don't sleep well.
If I drank coffee at night, I don't sleep well.

sections.summary: Using the First Conditional for a future possibility.
sections.explain: Use IF + Present Simple, WILL + base verb for a real future possibility.

words.word: If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay at home.
If it will rain tomorrow, we'll stay at home.
If it rains tomorrow, we stayed at home.

sections.explain: Do not normally use WILL in the IF-clause of a First Conditional.

words.word: If she calls, I will tell her.
If she will call, I will tell her.
If she calls, I tell her yesterday.

sections.explain: A First Conditional can use a negative Present Simple condition.

words.word: If we don't hurry, we'll miss the bus.
If we won't hurry, we'll miss the bus.
If we don't hurry, we miss the bus yesterday.

sections.summary: Using an imperative result in a real condition.
sections.explain: An IF-clause can be followed by an imperative for instructions.

words.word: If you feel tired, go to bed.
If you will feel tired, go to bed.
If you felt tired, go to bed every day.

sections.explain: Use the Zero Conditional when the result is generally or scientifically true.

words.word: If you don't water plants, they die.
If you won't water plants, they die.
If you didn't water plants, they always die now.

sections.explain: In a First Conditional, WILL normally appears in the result clause.

words.word: If I finish early, I'll call you.
If I'll finish early, I call you.
If I finish early, I called you.

sections.explain: A First Conditional can appear inside a question about a future possibility.

words.word: What will you do if you miss the train?
What do you will do if you miss the train?
What will you do if you will miss the train?

sections.explain: Use First Conditional when the situation concerns a specific possible future event.

words.word: If the weather is nice this weekend, we'll go to the beach.
If the weather will be nice this weekend, we'll go to the beach.
If the weather is nice this weekend, we went to the beach.
